newsitem.title: UK: Oil production to decline in 15 years, expert says.
newsitem.headline: Oil production to decline in 15 years, expert says.

text.p: World oil production will start to decline within 15 years if the rate of extraction remains at current levels, a U.S. geologist predicted on Wednesday.

The global economic catastrophe that would follow a decline in production can only be prevented by the development of an alternative fuel source, said Craig Bond Hatfield, a geologist at the University of Toledo in Ohio.
"The world will probably reach its maximum oil production rate in the next 15 years," he wrote in a commentary in the science journal Nature, recognised as an important world forum for such topics.
Even if demand does not grow, the decline in production would start by the year 2036, he said.
"In 1985, global oil consumption was 59.7 million barrels per day," Hatfield wrote. "By 1995 it was more than 69 million barrels per day."
This 16 percent increase was accounted for by members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

"Geological data indicate that, during the next 10 years, oil production outside OPEC countries will remain incapable of significant, sustained growth and is likely to begin a permanent decline during the first decade of the 21st century," he wrote.

New discoveries were not keeping pace with production, he added. "Globally, new discovery has averaged less than nine billion barrels per year since 1985 while consumption has averaged more than 23 billion barrels per year."
Hatfield examined known and estimated reserves and possibilities for new production and came to the conclusion that the oil was indeed drying up.
It could take 140 years for every drop to go -- as long as it took to get to this point, he said.

"But that's not a particularly important date because the exhaustion of the resource is only the end of a long, gradual decline in oil production which will last many decades," he said in a telephone interview.
"The really important event is the time when world oil production reaches its peak and begins to fall." This, he predicted, would come in 2011.
World demand for fuel will almost certainly be increasing as production declines, he said.
"The unprecedented economic growth of the world been based in part on the increased production of petroleum."
Once that stops, things could get bad.
"To get a feeling of the econonomic impact of the decline, all you have to do is remember the very minor and very temporary shortages we experienced in the 1970s.
"With a very minor shortfall in supply we experienced a several-fold increase in the price of oil that caused an increase in the price of everything else."
Inflation and a decline in the world economy followed.
"If you can envision that continuing on a permanent basis, with oil production declining every year, then you can appreciate the magnitude of the problem."
Increased fuel efficiency would provide a short-term answer but the real solution would be the development of a long-term substitute for oil.
"That is a Herculean task," Hatfield said, and noted work on synthetic fuels stopped to a great degree when oil prices stabilised in the 1980s.
"We desperately need to develop a more profound and sustained interest in a solution to problem because we don't have one," he said.
